claim: TaDa (Targeted DamID) entails expression of an RNA polymerase II subunit (RpII15) fused to the E. coli DNA adenine methyltransferase (Dam).
source: TaDa entails expression of an RNA polymerase II subunit (RpII15, hereafter PolII) fused to the E. coli DNA adenine methyltransferase (Dam).
evidence: The manuscript directly describes the molecular composition of the TaDa system.

claim: When bound to DNA, Dam:PolII methylates adenine within GATC motifs.
source: When bound to DNA, Dam:PolII methylates adenine within GATC motifs; enrichment of methylation at genes compared to free Dam control samples provides a measure of PolII occupancy, which is correlated with genes' transcriptional activity (Southall et al., 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: The mechanism of Dam:PolII action is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A, with citation to prior work.

claim: Enrichment of methylation at genes compared to free Dam control samples provides a measure of PolII occupancy, which is correlated with genes' transcriptional activity.
source: When bound to DNA, Dam:PolII methylates adenine within GATC motifs; enrichment of methylation at genes compared to free Dam control samples provides a measure of PolII occupancy, which is correlated with genes' transcriptional activity (Southall et al., 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: The relationship between methylation enrichment and transcriptional activity is stated with citation to Southall et al., 2013.

claim: TaDa datasets can provide information on chromatin accessibility (CATaDa).
source: In addition to indicating PolII occupancy within a given cell type, TaDa datasets can also provide information on chromatin accessibility (CATaDa) (Aughey et al., 2018; Figure 1A).
evidence: The capability of TaDa to provide chromatin accessibility information is stated with citation to Aughey et al., 2018.

claim: Analysis of the methylation patterns across the genome generated by untethered Dam is assumed to reflect the openness of chromatin, analogous to ATAC-seq datasets.
source: Analysis of the methylation patterns across the genome generated by untethered Dam is assumed to reflect the openness of chromatin, analogous to – and in good agreement with – ATAC-seq datasets (Aughey et al., 2018; Buenrostro et al., 2013).
evidence: The interpretation of Dam methylation patterns as reflecting chromatin openness is stated with citations to Aughey et al., 2018 and Buenrostro et al., 2013.

claim: The Drosophila nose (antenna) contains ~50 classes of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs).
source: The Drosophila nose (antenna) contains ~50 classes of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs), which develop from sensory organ precursor cells specified in the larval antennal imaginal disc (Barish and Volkan, 2015; Jefferis and Hummel, 2006; Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: The number of OSN classes is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: OSNs develop from sensory organ precursor cells specified in the larval antennal imaginal disc.
source: The Drosophila nose (antenna) contains ~50 classes of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs), which develop from sensory organ precursor cells specified in the larval antennal imaginal disc (Barish and Volkan, 2015; Jefferis and Hummel, 2006; Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: The developmental origin of OSNs is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Each OSN is characterized by the expression of a unique olfactory receptor (or, occasionally, receptors), of the Odorant Receptor (OR) or Ionotropic Receptor (IR) families.
source: Each OSN is characterized by the expression of a unique olfactory receptor (or, occasionally, receptors), of the Odorant Receptor (OR) or Ionotropic Receptor (IR) families.
evidence: The characteristic receptor expression pattern of OSNs is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Olfactory receptors function together with broadly expressed, family-specific co-receptors to define neuronal odor-response properties.
source: These proteins function – together with broadly expressed, family-specific co-receptors – to define neuronal odor-response properties (Benton, 2015; Gomez-Diaz et al., 2018; Robertson, 2019; Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: The functional role of receptors and co-receptors is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: The axons of all neurons expressing the same receptor(s) converge to a discrete and stereotyped glomerulus within the primary olfactory center (antennal lobe) in the brain.
source: Moreover, the axons of all neurons expressing the same receptor(s) converge to a discrete and stereotyped glomerulus within the primary olfactory center (antennal lobe) in the brain, where they synapse with both local interneurons (LNs) and projection neurons (PNs) (Brochtrup and Hummel, 2011; Hong and Luo, 2014; Jefferis and Hummel, 2006).
evidence: The axonal projection pattern of OSNs is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: OSN axons synapse with both local interneurons (LNs) and projection neurons (PNs) in the antennal lobe.
source: Moreover, the axons of all neurons expressing the same receptor(s) converge to a discrete and stereotyped glomerulus within the primary olfactory center (antennal lobe) in the brain, where they synapse with both local interneurons (LNs) and projection neurons (PNs) (Brochtrup and Hummel, 2011; Hong and Luo, 2014; Jefferis and Hummel, 2006).
evidence: The synaptic partners of OSNs are stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: OSNs are very small (~2–3 μm soma diameter).
source: However, the peripheral olfactory system of Drosophila poses several challenges to cell isolation: OSNs are very small (~2–3 μm soma diameter) and up to four neurons are tightly embedded under sensory sensilla (a porous cuticular hair that houses the neurons' dendrites) along with several support cells that seal each neuronal cluster from neighboring sensilla (Shanbhag et al., 1999; Shanbhag et al., 2000).
evidence: The size of OSN soma is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Up to four neurons are tightly embedded under sensory sensilla along with several support cells that seal each neuronal cluster from neighboring sensilla.
source: However, the peripheral olfactory system of Drosophila poses several challenges to cell isolation: OSNs are very small (~2–3 μm soma diameter) and up to four neurons are tightly embedded under sensory sensilla (a porous cuticular hair that houses the neurons' dendrites) along with several support cells that seal each neuronal cluster from neighboring sensilla (Shanbhag et al., 1999; Shanbhag et al., 2000).
evidence: The anatomical organization of OSNs within sensilla is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Each OSN class represents only a very small fraction of cells of the whole antenna, as few as 5–10 neurons of a total of ~3000 cells (both neuronal and non-neuronal).
source: Furthermore, each OSN class represents only a very small fraction of cells of the whole antenna, as few as 5–10 neurons of a total of ~3000 cells (both neuronal and non-neuronal) (Grabe et al., 2016; Shanbhag et al., 1999).
evidence: The proportion of each OSN class within the antenna is stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Ir64a promoter-Gal4 induction of Dam or Dam:PolII did not impact the expression or localization of the IR64a receptor.
source: We first verified that Ir64a promoter-Gal4 (hereafter, Ir64a-Gal4) induction of Dam or Dam:PolII did not impact the expression or localization of the IR64a receptor (Figure 1B) or the projection of these neurons to the antennal lobe (Figure 1C).
evidence: The lack of impact on IR64a expression and localization is stated and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ir64a-Gal4 induction of Dam or Dam:PolII did not impact the projection of Ir64a neurons to the antennal lobe.
source: We first verified that Ir64a promoter-Gal4 (hereafter, Ir64a-Gal4) induction of Dam or Dam:PolII did not impact the expression or localization of the IR64a receptor (Figure 1B) or the projection of these neurons to the antennal lobe (Figure 1C).
evidence: The lack of impact on neuronal projections is stated and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dam:PolII consistently accessed the Ir64a gene region at higher levels than Dam alone, particularly near the 5' end of the locus.
source: As a positive control, we first examined the mapping of reads of methylated DNA fragments to the Ir64a gene. Dam:PolII consistently accessed this gene region at higher levels than Dam alone, particularly near the 5' end of the locus (Figure 1D), consistent with previously described genome-wide PolII occupancy patterns (Southall et al., 2013).
evidence: The differential access of Dam:PolII versus Dam to the Ir64a gene is stated and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The enrichment of Dam:PolII access to the Ir64a gene was specific to the Ir64a neurons.
source: As expected, the enrichment of Dam:PolII access to the Ir64a gene was specific to the Ir64a neurons (Figure 1E).
evidence: The specificity of Ir64a gene enrichment to Ir64a neurons is stated and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In Ir64a neurons, the Ir64a gene OS was significantly positive (OS = 0.20; False Discovery Rate (FDR) = 4.26e-10).
source: In Ir64a neurons, the Ir64a gene OS was significantly positive (OS = 0.20; False Discovery Rate (FDR) = 4.26e-10), while it was not significantly different from zero in the other six neuron populations (Figure 1E, bottom).
evidence: The occupancy score and statistical significance for Ir64a in Ir64a neurons is stated with specific values.

claim: The Ir64a gene OS was not significantly different from zero in the six other neuron populations (Ir31a, Ir40a, Ir75a, Ir75b, Ir75c, Ir84a).
source: In Ir64a neurons, the Ir64a gene OS was significantly positive (OS = 0.20; False Discovery Rate (FDR) = 4.26e-10), while it was not significantly different from zero in the other six neuron populations (Figure 1E, bottom).
evidence: The lack of significant occupancy score for Ir64a in other neuron populations is stated.

claim: OSs for other Ir genes were significantly positive in the corresponding neuronal population, but not in those in which the receptors are not expressed.
source: Similarly, OSs for other Ir genes were significantly positive in the corresponding neuronal population, but not in those in which the receptors are not expressed (Figure 1F).
evidence: The pattern of Ir gene occupancy scores across populations is stated and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In Ir31a neurons, Ir40a had a positive OS (0.12; FDR = 1.93e-13), although it was much lower than that of Ir31a (OS = 0.41; FDR = 2.67e-6).
source: We noted two exceptions: first, in Ir31a neurons, Ir40a had a positive OS (0.12; FDR = 1.93e-13), although it was much lower than that of Ir31a (OS = 0.41; FDR = 2.67e-6) (Figure 1F).
evidence: The occupancy scores for Ir40a and Ir31a in Ir31a neurons are stated with specific values.

claim: The Ir75a, Ir75b, and Ir75c genes had positive OSs in all three of the corresponding neuron populations.
source: Second, the Ir75a, Ir75b, and Ir75c genes had positive OSs in all three of the corresponding neuron populations (Figure 1F).
evidence: The pattern of occupancy scores for Ir75a/b/c genes is stated and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The positive OSs for Ir75a, Ir75b, and Ir75c in all three corresponding neuron populations is most likely due to these tandemly clustered genes having overlapping transcription units.
source: As the proteins they encode (and the corresponding Ir-Gal4 drivers) are expressed in discrete neuron populations, this latter result is most likely due to these tandemly clustered genes having overlapping transcription units (Prieto-Godino et al., 2017).
evidence: The interpretation of the Ir75a/b/c occupancy pattern is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Ir8a has a significant OS in all Ir populations except for Ir40a neurons.
source: Ir8a has a significant OS in all Ir populations except for Ir40a neurons, which is consistent with the selective expression and function of IR8a in acid-sensing OSNs but not hygrosensory neurons (Abuin et al., 2011; Figure 1F).
evidence: The pattern of Ir8a occupancy across populations is stated and shown in Figure 1F, with citation to prior work.

claim: IR8a is selectively expressed and functions in acid-sensing OSNs but not hygrosensory neurons.
source: Ir8a has a significant OS in all Ir populations except for Ir40a neurons, which is consistent with the selective expression and function of IR8a in acid-sensing OSNs but not hygrosensory neurons (Abuin et al., 2011; Figure 1F).
evidence: The expression and function of IR8a is stated with citation to Abuin et al., 2011.

claim: IR25a is broadly expressed in most antennal neurons.
source: IR25a is broadly expressed in most antennal neurons (Abuin et al., 2011; Benton et al., 2009) – although it may have a role in only a subset of these – which is reflected in a significant OS for Ir25a in all seven populations (Figure 1F).
evidence: The expression pattern of IR25a is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Ir25a has a significant OS in all seven Ir neuron populations.
source: IR25a is broadly expressed in most antennal neurons (Abuin et al., 2011; Benton et al., 2009) – although it may have a role in only a subset of these – which is reflected in a significant OS for Ir25a in all seven populations (Figure 1F).
evidence: The occupancy score pattern for Ir25a is stated and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: IR40a is co-expressed with another receptor, IR93a.
source: IR40a is co-expressed with another receptor, IR93a (Enjin et al., 2016; Knecht et al., 2016), although Ir40a neurons display significant occupancy of Ir93a, several other Ir populations also have, unexpectedly, a significant OS for this gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The co-expression of IR40a and IR93a is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Two broadly-expressed neuronal genes, elav and nSyb, display significant OSs across Ir neuron populations.
source: Two broadly-expressed neuronal genes, elav and nSyb, display significant OSs across populations, as does pebbled (peb), a molecular marker for OSNs (Sweeney et al., 2007).
evidence: The occupancy scores for elav and nSyb are stated and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Pebbled (peb), a molecular marker for OSNs, displays significant OSs across Ir neuron populations.
source: Two broadly-expressed neuronal genes, elav and nSyb, display significant OSs across populations, as does pebbled (peb), a molecular marker for OSNs (Sweeney et al., 2007).
evidence: The occupancy score for peb is stated and shown in Figure 1G, with citation to prior work.

claim: Oaz, a broad marker of PNs, is not significantly occupied in Ir neuron populations.
source: By contrast, oaz, a broad marker of PNs (Hong et al., 2009), is not significantly occupied.
evidence: The lack of occupancy for oaz is stated and shown in Figure 1G, with citation to prior work.

claim: Obp59a and Obp84a are expressed in sensilla housing Ir neurons.
source: Two of these, Obp59a and Obp84a are expressed in sensilla housing Ir neurons (Larter et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2018a), but neither of these genes displays significant OSs in any neuron population (Figure 1G).
evidence: The expression of Obp59a and Obp84a is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Neither Obp59a nor Obp84a displays significant OSs in any Ir neuron population.
source: Two of these, Obp59a and Obp84a are expressed in sensilla housing Ir neurons (Larter et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2018a), but neither of these genes displays significant OSs in any neuron population (Figure 1G).
evidence: The lack of occupancy scores for Obp59a and Obp84a is stated and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Antennal OSNs are cholinergic.
source: Electrophysiological experiments indicate that antennal OSNs are cholinergic (Kazama and Wilson, 2008).
evidence: The neurotransmitter identity of OSNs is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Genes encoding the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) and choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) have significant OSs in all Ir neuron populations.
source: In line with this functional property, genes encoding the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) and choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) have significant OSs in all populations, while glutamatergic and GABAergic neuron markers (vesicular glutamate transporter (VGlut) and glutamic acid decarboxylase 1 (Gad1)) do not (Figure 1G).
evidence: The occupancy scores for VAChT and ChAT are stated and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Glutamatergic and GABAergic neuron markers (VGlut and Gad1) do not have significant OSs in Ir neuron populations.
source: In line with this functional property, genes encoding the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) and choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) have significant OSs in all populations, while glutamatergic and GABAergic neuron markers (vesicular glutamate transporter (VGlut) and glutamic acid decarboxylase 1 (Gad1)) do not (Figure 1G).
evidence: The lack of occupancy scores for VGlut and Gad1 is stated and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A GABA receptor subunit (encoded by GABA-B-R2) displays significant, but variable, OSs in different Ir populations.
source: We note, however, that a GABA receptor subunit (encoded by GABA-B-R2) – which is heterogeneously expressed and mediates population-specific presynaptic gain control in different Or OSNs (Root et al., 2008) – displays significant, but variable, OSs in different Ir populations (Figure 1G).
evidence: The occupancy scores for GABA-B-R2 are stated and shown in Figure 1G, with citation to prior work.

claim: Only one neuropeptide detected in the antennal lobe by proteomics, short neuropeptide F (sNPF), originates from OSNs.
source: Finally, of the multiple neuropeptides detected in the antennal lobe by proteomics, only one, short neuropeptide F (sNPF), originates from OSNs (Carlsson et al., 2010), where it has a role in glomerular-specific presynaptic facilitation (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: The OSN-specific expression of sNPF is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: sNPF has a role in glomerular-specific presynaptic facilitation in OSNs.
source: Finally, of the multiple neuropeptides detected in the antennal lobe by proteomics, only one, short neuropeptide F (sNPF), originates from OSNs (Carlsson et al., 2010), where it has a role in glomerular-specific presynaptic facilitation (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: The functional role of sNPF is stated with citation to Root et al., 2011.

claim: Significant (and heterogeneous) OSs are observed for sNPF in Ir neuron populations.
source: Consistently, we observe significant (and heterogeneous) OSs for sNPF, but not for genes encoding neuropeptides whose presence in the antennal lobe derives from expression in central neurons (e.g. Tachykinin [Tk], Myoinhibiting peptide [Mip]) (Carlsson et al., 2010).

claim: Genes encoding neuropeptides whose presence in the antennal lobe derives from expression in central neurons (e.g. Tachykinin [Tk], Myoinhibiting peptide [Mip]) do not have significant OSs in Ir neuron populations.
source: Consistently, we observe significant (and heterogeneous) OSs for sNPF, but not for genes encoding neuropeptides whose presence in the antennal lobe derives from expression in central neurons (e.g. Tachykinin [Tk], Myoinhibiting peptide [Mip]) (Carlsson et al., 2010).
evidence: The lack of occupancy scores for Tk and Mip is stated and shown in Figure 1G, with citation to prior work.

claim: The number of genes significantly occupied by PolII ranged from 3603 to 4775 across the seven Ir neuron datasets, representing 20–27% of all genes.
source: The number of genes significantly occupied by PolII ranged from 3603 to 4775 across the seven datasets, representing 20–27% of all genes (Figure 2A and Supplementary files 1–3).

source: This analysis revealed an interesting correspondence in the clustering of OSs with the phylogeny of the corresponding receptor genes (Prieto-Godino et al., 2017): neurons expressing the most recently duplicated receptor genes, Ir75b and Ir75c, were clustered together.

claim: Neurons expressing the most recently duplicated receptor genes, Ir75b and Ir75c, were clustered together in hierarchical clustering of OSs.
source: This analysis revealed an interesting correspondence in the clustering of OSs with the phylogeny of the corresponding receptor genes (Prieto-Godino et al., 2017): neurons expressing the most recently duplicated receptor genes, Ir75b and Ir75c, were clustered together.

claim: The next most similar neuron population to Ir75b and Ir75c expresses Ir75a, which is the likely ancestral member of this tandem gene array.

claim: Ir40a and Ir64a neurons clustered together away from the other acid-sensing populations.
source: Ir40a and Ir64a neurons clustered together away from the other acid-sensing populations, possibly reflecting the development of these neurons within the sacculus, rather than in sensilla located on the antennal surface.

claim: The clustering of Ir40a and Ir64a neurons together possibly reflects the development of these neurons within the sacculus, rather than in sensilla located on the antennal surface.

claim: Each Ir neuron population displays PolII occupancy of a distinct combination of 18–31 GPCR genes (out of 111).

claim: Individual Ir neuron datasets had very few or no unique neuron projection guidance genes.
source: While each neuron population had a unique combination of many dozens of PolII-occupied genes, individual datasets had very few or no unique genes (Figure 2F and Supplementary file 17).

claim: Individual Ir OSN classes had 190–286 occupied transcription factor genes.

claim: There was considerable variation in Dam:PolII occupancy of transcription factor genes across the Ir neuron populations.
source: There was considerable variation in Dam:PolII occupancy of transcription factor genes across the neuron populations (Figure 2G), consistent with each neuronal subtype possessing a unique and complex gene regulatory network to support its specific differentiation properties.

claim: Each neuronal subtype possesses a unique and complex gene regulatory network to support its specific differentiation properties.
source: There was considerable variation in Dam:PolII occupancy of transcription factor genes across the neuron populations (Figure 2G), consistent with each neuronal subtype possessing a unique and complex gene regulatory network to support its specific differentiation properties.

source: By contrast, Ir75a neurons had a single uniquely occupied transcription factor gene (pou domain motif 3 (pdm3), investigated further below).

evidence: The proportion of differentially occupied genes is stated.

claim: The subset of 1694 differentially occupied genes encompasses all of the expected Ir genes.
source: This number is likely to be an overestimate as it includes overlapping and/or intronic genes that, as described above, cannot be parsed further using TaDa data. Importantly, this subset encompasses all of the expected Ir genes (see Figure 4D).
evidence: The inclusion of expected Ir genes in the differentially occupied set is stated and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Comparisons among the closely clustered Ir75a, Ir75b, and Ir75c neuron datasets result in very few of the total differences (0.4–1.7%).
source: For example, comparisons among the closely clustered Ir75a, Ir75b, and Ir75c neuron datasets result in very few of the total differences (0.4–1.7%).
evidence: The proportion of differences among Ir75a/b/c neurons is stated and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Slightly more than half (51%) of the total differences in the Ir84a neuron dataset arise from comparisons with the distantly clustered Ir40a neuron dataset.
source: Conversely, slightly more than half (51%) of the total differences in the Ir84a neuron dataset arise from comparisons with the distantly clustered Ir40a neuron dataset.
evidence: The proportion of differences between Ir84a and Ir40a neurons is stated and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis of the 1694 differentially occupied genes showed highly significant enrichment in neuron, neural development, and signaling categories.
source: We investigated the general characteristics of the 1694 differentially occupied genes by performing Gene Ontology analyses, finding highly significant enrichment in neuron, neural development, and signaling categories (Figure 4C).
evidence: The GO enrichment results are stated and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The enrichment of differentially occupied genes in neuron, neural development, and signaling categories is consistent with these genes underlying the known unique anatomical and physiological properties of these neuron classes.
source: This enrichment is consistent with these genes underlying the known unique anatomical and physiological properties of these neuron classes, and indicates that our comparative TaDa approach would be valuable in identifying candidates that contribute functionally to these properties.
evidence: The interpretation of the GO enrichment is stated.

claim: pdm3 has a significant OS only in Ir75a neurons.
source: The robust signal displayed by pdm3 for between-population differences is consistent with this gene having a significant OS only in Ir75a neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: The occupancy score for pdm3 is stated and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: pdm3 is the sole transcription factor gene that is uniquely occupied in Ir75a neuron population.
source: Notably, from the global survey, pdm3 is the sole transcription factor gene that is uniquely occupied in this neuron population (Figure 2G and Supplementary file 20).
evidence: The unique occupancy of pdm3 in Ir75a neurons is stated.

claim: Pdm3 is a nervous-system enriched transcription factor.
source: Pdm3 is a nervous-system enriched transcription factor (Brown et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2012; Tichy et al., 2008), although its precise in vivo binding specificity is unknown.
evidence: The expression pattern of Pdm3 is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: In the maxillary palp, Pdm3 is expressed in multiple classes of Or neurons and functions in controlling receptor expression and axon guidance.
source: In another olfactory organ, the maxillary palp, Pdm3 is expressed in multiple classes of Or neurons and functions in controlling receptor expression and axon guidance (Tichy et al., 2008), but its role in Ir neurons is unknown.
evidence: The function of Pdm3 in the maxillary palp is stated with citation to Tichy et al., 2008.

claim: Only Ir75a neurons displayed robust nuclear Pdm3 immunofluorescence, although a subset of Ir40a neurons had above-background signals.
source: Using Pdm3 antibodies, we first analyzed protein expression in antennae in which we co-labeled each of the Ir populations with the driver lines used in the TaDa experiments. Only Ir75a neurons displayed robust nuclear Pdm3 immunofluorescence, although a subset of Ir40a neurons had above-background signals (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The Pdm3 protein expression pattern is stated and shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: peb-Gal4-driven pdm3RNAi led to loss of most IR75a expression, with the remaining detectable neurons expressing very low levels of this receptor.
source: peb-Gal4-driven pdm3RNAi (peb>pdm3RNAi) led to loss of most IR75a expression, with the remaining detectable neurons expressing very low levels of this receptor (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: The effect of pdm3 RNAi on IR75a expression is stated and shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: Robust expression of all other Irs was maintained in peb>pdm3RNAi antennae.
source: By contrast, robust expression of all other Irs was maintained (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: The maintenance of other Ir expression is stated and shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: The number of cells expressing IR75b increased in pdm3RNAi antennae.
source: We noted, however, that the number of cells expressing IR75b increased in pdm3RNAi antennae (Figure 5D).
evidence: The increase in IR75b-expressing cells is stated and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Pdm3 functions (directly or indirectly) to promote IR75a expression and repress IR75b expression.
source: These observations suggest that Pdm3 functions (directly or indirectly) to promote IR75a expression and repress IR75b expression.
evidence: The interpretation of the pdm3 RNAi effects is stated.

claim: The novel IR75b-expressing cells in pdm3RNAi antennae are mainly located in the proximal region of the antenna near the sacculus, where Ir75a neurons are normally found.
source: The novel IR75b-expressing cells in pdm3RNAi antennae are mainly located in the proximal region of the antenna near the sacculus, where Ir75a neurons are normally found (Figure 6A).
evidence: The location of ectopic IR75b-expressing cells is stated and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Loss of Pdm3 results in a switch of receptor expression from IR75a to IR75b.
source: This distribution suggested that loss of Pdm3 results in a switch of receptor expression from IR75a to IR75b.
evidence: The interpretation of the ectopic IR75b expression is stated.

claim: Both Ir75a-GFP and Ir75b-GFP transgenes are faithfully expressed in IR75a and IR75b protein-expressing neurons.
source: We investigated this possibility by examining the activity of transcriptional reporters for these receptors, encompassing minimal regulatory DNA sequences fused to CD4:tdGFP (hereafter, GFP) (Prieto-Godino et al., 2017). Both Ir75a-GFP and Ir75b-GFP transgenes are faithfully expressed in IR75a and IR75b protein-expressing neurons (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: The faithful expression of Ir-GFP reporters is stated and shown in Figure 6B–C.

claim: In pdm3RNAi antennae Ir75a-GFP expression is greatly diminished, while Ir75b-GFP is expressed in many ectopic cells.
source: In pdm3RNAi antennae Ir75a-GFP expression is greatly diminished, while Ir75b-GFP is expressed in many ectopic cells (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: The effect of pdm3 RNAi on Ir-GFP reporter expression is stated and shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: In pdm3RNAi animals the Ir75a-GFP DP1l signal is almost completely lost.
source: In pdm3RNAi animals the Ir75a-GFP DP1l signal is almost completely lost (Figure 6E), consistent with the reduction in reporter expression in antennae.
evidence: The loss of Ir75a-GFP signal in DP1l is stated and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In pdm3RNAi animals the Ir75b-GFP signal in the DL2d glomerulus is greatly intensified, and the glomerulus is enlarged.
source: By contrast, the Ir75b-GFP signal in the DL2d glomerulus is greatly intensified, and the glomerulus is enlarged (Figure 6E), presumably reflecting the increased number of Ir75b neurons (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: The intensification and enlargement of Ir75b-GFP signal in DL2d is stated and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In the absence of Pdm3, Ir75a neurons adopt Ir75b neuron fate including both receptor identity and glomerular innervation pattern.
source: The simplest interpretation of these observations is that in the absence of Pdm3, Ir75a neurons adopt Ir75b neuron fate including both receptor identity and glomerular innervation pattern.
evidence: The interpretation of the pdm3 RNAi phenotype is stated.

claim: The expression of Pdm3 in Ir75a neurons in adult antennae suggests that it has a persistent role in these cells.
source: While OSN fate is established in early pupae (Barish and Volkan, 2015; Jefferis and Hummel, 2006; Yan et al., 2020), the expression of Pdm3 in Ir75a neurons in adult antennae (Figure 5A–B) suggests that it has a persistent role in these cells.
evidence: The persistent expression of Pdm3 in adults is stated and shown in Figure 5A–B, with citations to prior work.

claim: When pdm3RNAi was induced only in adults (through a 19°C to 29°C temperature shift after eclosion) the same increase in Ir75b expression and decrease in Ir75a expression was observed.
source: When pdm3RNAi was induced only in adults (through a 19°C to 29°C temperature shift after eclosion) the same increase in Ir75b expression and decrease in Ir75a expression was observed (Figure 6F).
evidence: The effect of adult-only pdm3 RNAi is stated and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Several cells expressing both IR75b and IR75a were detected in adult-only pdm3RNAi antennae, which are never observed in non-RNAi antennae.
source: Notably, we detected several cells expressing both IR75b and IR75a, which are never observed in non-RNAi antennae (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: The co-expression of IR75a and IR75b is stated and shown in Figure 6G–H.

claim: Pdm3 has a persistent role in mature Ir75a neurons to repress Ir75b expression and promote Ir75a expression.
source: These observations indicate that Pdm3 has a persistent role in mature Ir75a neurons to repress Ir75b expression and promote Ir75a expression.
evidence: The interpretation of the adult-only pdm3 RNAi results is stated.

claim: In adult-only pdm3RNAi animals Ir75b-GFP signal was detected both in DL2d and DP1l neurons.
source: The ectopic expression of Ir75b in Ir75a OSNs was confirmed by examining the projection of Ir75b-GFP-expressing neurons: in adult-only pdm3RNAi animals – but not in control pan-developmental pdm3RNAi – Ir75b-GFP signal was detected both in DL2d and DP1l neurons (Figure 6I).
evidence: The ectopic Ir75b-GFP signal in DP1l is stated and shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Late loss of pdm3 leads to misexpression of Ir75b-GFP in Ir75a neurons after they have targeted to DP1l.
source: This observation is consistent with late loss of pdm3 leading to misexpression of Ir75b-GFP in Ir75a neurons after they have targeted to DP1l.
evidence: The interpretation of the ectopic Ir75b-GFP signal in DP1l is stated.

claim: At mid-pupal stages (48 hr APF), only trace levels of Fmi immunoreactivity were observed across OSN soma.
source: We first examined antennae from mid-pupal stages (48 hr APF) but observed only trace levels of immunoreactivity across OSN soma (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The low Fmi signal in OSN soma at 48 hr APF is stated and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 24 hr APF, Fmi signal was slightly stronger in OSN soma, but much more prominent in the OSN axons as they left the antenna.
source: At 24 hr APF, this signal was slightly stronger, but much more prominent in the OSN axons as they left the antenna (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that this protein is predominantly transported to the axonal compartment of these neurons.
evidence: The Fmi signal in OSN axons at 24 hr APF is stated and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Fmi protein is predominantly transported to the axonal compartment of OSNs.
source: At 24 hr APF, this signal was slightly stronger, but much more prominent in the OSN axons as they left the antenna (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that this protein is predominantly transported to the axonal compartment of these neurons.
evidence: The interpretation of the Fmi localization is stated.

claim: Fmi protein was strongly detected in the OSN axons as they enter the antennal lobe at 24 hr APF.
source: Indeed, Fmi protein was strongly detected in the OSN axons as they enter the antennal lobe at 24 hr APF (Figure 7A).
evidence: The Fmi signal in OSN axons entering the antennal lobe is stated and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Fmi was still robustly expressed at 48 hr APF as OSNs coalesced onto individual glomeruli with broad, but slightly heterogeneous, expression in glomeruli across the antennal lobe.
source: Fmi was still robustly expressed at 48 hr APF as OSNs coalesced onto individual glomeruli with broad, but slightly heterogeneous, expression in glomeruli across the antennal lobe (Figure 7A).
evidence: The Fmi expression at 48 hr APF is stated and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Fmi levels began to decrease to undetectable levels in some glomeruli in the adult stage, while persisting in others.
source: Subsequently, Fmi levels began to decrease to undetectable levels in some glomeruli in the adult stage, while persisting in others (Figure 7B).
evidence: The heterogeneous Fmi expression in adult glomeruli is stated and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Fmi was detected in DL2d (Ir75b) and DL2v (Ir75c), but not the neighboring DP1l (Ir75a).
source: Most of these glomeruli are innervated by Or neurons, but we could detect Fmi in DL2d (Ir75b) and DL2v (Ir75c), but not the neighboring DP1l (Ir75a) (Figure 7B), in partial concordance with the TaDa data (Figure 4E).
evidence: The Fmi expression in specific glomeruli is stated and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: From later developmental stages (~48 hr APF), Fmi was also detected in a group of ~16 cells located on the antero-dorsal region of the antennal lobe.
source: From later developmental stages (~48 hr APF), Fmi was also detected in a group of ~16 cells located on the antero-dorsal region of the antennal lobe (Figure 7A).
evidence: The Fmi expression in cells adjacent to the antennal lobe is stated and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The ~16 Fmi-positive cells located on the antero-dorsal region of the antennal lobe are likely to be LNs, based upon their expression of Elav and presence of stained processes that innervate the antennal lobe but do not project to higher olfactory centers.
source: These cells are likely to be LNs, based upon their expression of Elav (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) and presence of stained processes that innervate the antennal lobe but do not project to higher olfactory centers.
evidence: The identification of Fmi-positive cells as LNs is stated and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At mid-pupal development (48 hr APF), differential glomerular expression of Fmi was much more marked in LN>fmiRNAi animals compared to control animals.
source: At mid-pupal development (48 hr APF), differential glomerular expression of Fmi was much more marked compared to control animals (Figure 7C).
evidence: The differential Fmi expression in LN>fmiRNAi animals is stated and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Fmi is dynamically expressed in different populations of OSNs during development.
source: Although we could not confidently define all glomerular identities at this earlier developmental stage, prior to full maturation of the antennal lobe, Fmi protein levels did not appear to correspond precisely with the TaDa OSs (e.g. the VL2a glomerulus, innervated by Ir84a neurons, was not devoid of Fmi signal). This observation suggests that Fmi is dynamically expressed in different populations of OSNs during development.
evidence: The interpretation of the Fmi expression pattern is stated.

claim: The antennal lobes of constitutive fmi RNAi animals showed fully penetrant, severe morphological defects: the stereotyped glomerular boundaries observed in the lobes of control animals were mostly lacking, with only a few, large glomerulus-like subregions detected.
source: The antennal lobes of these animals showed fully penetrant, severe morphological defects: the stereotyped glomerular boundaries observed in the lobes of control animals were mostly lacking, with only a few, large glomerulus-like subregions detected (Figure 8A).
evidence: The antennal lobe morphological defects in fmi RNAi animals are stated and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The fmi RNAi phenotype was reproduced with an independent RNAi line that targets a distinct region of the coding sequence.
source: This phenotype was reproduced with an independent RNAi line that targets a distinct region of the coding sequence (Figure 8A).
evidence: The reproducibility of the fmi RNAi phenotype is stated and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Neurons labeled by Ir75a-GFP, Ir75b-GFP, or Ir75c-GFP were no longer constrained to discrete glomeruli in fmi RNAi animals.
source: Neurons labeled by Ir75a-GFP, Ir75b-GFP, or Ir75c-GFP were no longer constrained to discrete glomeruli (Figure 8B), although the mistargeting was relatively mild within the antennal lobe as a whole.
evidence: The mistargeting of Ir neurons in fmi RNAi animals is stated and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The limited defects of individual neuron populations in fmi RNAi animals suggests that the lack of Fmi does not disrupt long-range targeting properties of OSNs, but rather impacts local segregation of OSNs.
source: The limited defects of individual neuron populations suggests that the lack of Fmi does not disrupt long-range targeting properties of OSNs, but rather impacts local segregation of OSNs.
evidence: The interpretation of the fmi RNAi phenotype is stated.

claim: Double labeling of neurons that normally project to adjacent glomeruli (Ir75a-GFP and Ir75b-Tom; Ir84a-GFP and Ir31a-Tom) revealed frequent overlap between these normally-segregated populations in fmi RNAi animals.
source: Consistently, double labeling of neurons that normally project to adjacent glomeruli (Ir75a-GFP and Ir75b-Tomato (Tom); Ir84a-GFP and Ir31a-Tom) revealed frequent overlap between these normally-segregated populations (Figure 8C).
evidence: The overlap of normally-segregated populations in fmi RNAi animals is stated and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: OSN-specific fmi RNAi using peb-Gal4 produced an equally strong defect in antennal lobe glomerular segregation as constitutive fmi RNAi.
source: To limit fmi RNAi to OSNs, we used peb-Gal4, which produced an equally strong defect in antennal lobe glomerular segregation (Figure 8D).
evidence: The OSN-specific fmi RNAi phenotype is stated and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: LN>fmiRNAi animals did not exhibit antennal lobe morphological defects.
source: This LN source of Fmi does not appear to contribute to glomerulus formation as LN>fmiRNAi animals did not exhibit antennal lobe morphological defects (Figure 8D).
evidence: The lack of phenotype in LN>fmiRNAi animals is stated and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: PN>fmiRNAi animals had normal antennal lobe morphology.
source: Similarly, when we targeted fmi to the synaptic partners of OSNs, the PNs – which pre-pattern the glomerular organization of the antennal lobe (Jefferis and Hummel, 2006) – using the GH146 driver, antennal lobe morphology appeared normal (Figure 8D).
evidence: The lack of phenotype in PN>fmiRNAi animals is stated and shown in Figure 8D, with citation to prior work.

claim: Fmi functions principally, if not exclusively, within OSNs for correct glomerulus formation.
source: Together, these results indicate that Fmi functions principally, if not exclusively, within OSNs for correct glomerulus formation.
evidence: The interpretation of the cell type-specific fmi RNAi results is stated.

claim: When animals were shifted from 19°C to 29°C at 10 hr APF (prior to initial expression of peb-Gal4), all animals displayed antennal lobe morphological defects of varying degrees, and Ir75b-GFP-labeled neurons did not coalesce to a discrete glomerular unit.
source: When animals were shifted from 19°C to 29°C at 10 hr APF (prior to initial expression of peb-Gal4), all animals displayed antennal lobe morphological defects of varying degrees, and Ir75b-GFP-labeled neurons did not coalesce to a discrete glomerular unit (Figure 8E).
evidence: The effect of early fmi RNAi induction is stated and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: When animals were shifted from 19°C to 29°C at 20 hr APF, the severity of the fmi RNAi phenotype was diminished.
source: When shifted at 20 hr APF, the severity of the phenotype was diminished (Figure 8E).
evidence: The effect of intermediate fmi RNAi induction is stated and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: When animals were shifted from 19°C to 29°C at 40 hr APF, the antennal lobe and Ir75b neuron targeting were indistinguishable from controls.
source: When shifted at 40 hr APF, the antennal lobe and Ir75b neuron targeting were indistinguishable from controls (Figure 8E).
evidence: The lack of effect of late fmi RNAi induction is stated and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Fmi has an early developmental function in OSN axon targeting.
source: These experiments indicate an early developmental function for Fmi.
evidence: The interpretation of the temporal fmi RNAi results is stated.

claim: In peb>fmiRNAi animals, OSNs reach the antennal lobe, but bundle organization is highly disrupted, with subsets of axons apparently defasciculating prematurely in the central area of the lobe.
source: In peb>fmiRNAi animals, OSNs reach the antennal lobe, but bundle organization is highly disrupted, with subsets of axons apparently defasciculating prematurely in the central area of the lobe (Figure 8F).
evidence: The OSN axon bundle defects in fmi RNAi animals are stated and shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Mutations in two core components of the planar cell polarity pathway, frizzled and dishevelled, had no apparent impact on antennal lobe formation.
source: Mutations in two core components of the planar cell polarity pathway, frizzled and dishevelled (Usui et al., 1999), had no apparent impact on antennal lobe formation.
evidence: The lack of phenotype in frizzled and dishevelled mutants is stated and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1, with citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of frazzled (encoding a Netrin homolog which function with Fmi in midline axon guidance) did not reproduce the fmi phenotype.
source: Similarly, loss of frazzled (encoding a Netrin homolog which function with Fmi in midline axon guidance [Organisti et al., 2015]), golden goal (with which Fmi collaborates in photoreceptor axon guidance [Hakeda-Suzuki et al., 2011]), or espinas (which encodes a LIM domain protein that binds Fmi intracellularly and functions in dendrite self-avoidance [Matsubara et al., 2011]) did not reproduce the fmi phenotype.
evidence: The lack of phenotype in frazzled mutants is stated and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1, with citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of golden goal (with which Fmi collaborates in photoreceptor axon guidance) did not reproduce the fmi phenotype.
source: Similarly, loss of frazzled (encoding a Netrin homolog which function with Fmi in midline axon guidance [Organisti et al., 2015]), golden goal (with which Fmi collaborates in photoreceptor axon guidance [Hakeda-Suzuki et al., 2011]), or espinas (which encodes a LIM domain protein that binds Fmi intracellularly and functions in dendrite self-avoidance [Matsubara et al., 2011]) did not reproduce the fmi phenotype.
evidence: The lack of phenotype in golden goal mutants is stated and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1, with citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of espinas (which encodes a LIM domain protein that binds Fmi intracellularly and functions in dendrite self-avoidance) did not reproduce the fmi phenotype.
source: Similarly, loss of frazzled (encoding a Netrin homolog which function with Fmi in midline axon guidance [Organisti et al., 2015]), golden goal (with which Fmi collaborates in photoreceptor axon guidance [Hakeda-Suzuki et al., 2011]), or espinas (which encodes a LIM domain protein that binds Fmi intracellularly and functions in dendrite self-avoidance [Matsubara et al., 2011]) did not reproduce the fmi phenotype.
evidence: The lack of phenotype in espinas mutants is stated and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1, with citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of Gαq (through which the Fmi GPCR-domain has been suggested to act to regulate dendrite growth) did not reproduce the fmi phenotype in OSNs.
source: Finally, although the intracellular signaling mechanism of Fmi is not well understood, the Fmi GPCR-domain has been suggested to act through the Gαq subunit to regulate dendrite growth (Wang et al., 2016); however, we found no evidence that this signaling mechanism operates in OSNs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The lack of phenotype in Gαq mutants is stated and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1, with citation to prior work.

claim: Fmi functions through other cellular mechanisms to control OSN axon segregation.
source: These observations suggest that Fmi functions through other cellular mechanisms to control OSN axon segregation.
evidence: The interpretation of the genetic interaction results is stated.

claim: Reproducibility among all triplicate TaDa datasets (average r2 = 0.85) was consistent with previous TaDa studies.
source: Reproducibility among all triplicate datasets (average r2 = 0.85) was consistent with previous TaDa studies (Southall et al., 2013).
evidence: The reproducibility of TaDa datasets is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: The Ir64a population comprises ~16 neurons that are housed in sensilla in the sacculus, where they detect acidic odors.
source: To test the feasibility of TaDa for profiling Drosophila OSNs, we first focused on the Ir64a population, which comprises ~16 neurons that are housed in sensilla in the sacculus (a chamber within the antenna), where they detect acidic odors (Ai et al., 2010).
evidence: The characteristics of Ir64a neurons are stated with citation to Ai et al., 2010.

claim: The TaDa experimental design is expected to integrate PolII occupancy patterns from the mid-pupal stage (when Ir-Gal4 expression initiates) to adults.
source: This experimental design is expected to integrate PolII occupancy patterns from the mid-pupal stage (when Ir-Gal4 expression initiates) to adults.
evidence: The temporal scope of TaDa profiling is stated.

claim: The analyzed Ir populations range from ~8 to ~25 cells per antenna.
source: We extended the TaDa approach using drivers to target six additional individual OSN classes, including all acid-sensing Ir populations (Ir31a, Ir75a, Ir75b, Ir75c, Ir84a) (Grosjean et al., 2011; Silbering et al., 2011), as well as the hygrosensory Ir40a neurons (Enjin et al., 2016; Knecht et al., 2016); these populations range from ~8 to ~25 cells per antenna (Knecht et al., 2016; Prieto-Godino et al., 2017).
evidence: The size of Ir neuron populations is stated with citations to prior work.
